A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AudioSeg study. All 19 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, support comparison. Retained content can be matched across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original YTSeg experiments comparing segmentation models, acoustic features and inference strategies, alongside ablations and failure analyses (Tables 4–7 and A1–A6).

after.justification: V2 retains these experiments and adds original AMI, timestamp-prediction, title-quality and evaluation-sensitivity results (Table 7 and Tables A5–A11).

M1.justification: Section 3.4.1 adds MLLM inference formulations producing timestamps and titles, either directly or alongside transcription. These extend the output procedure. AudioSeg's architecture, feature fusion and existing training objectives remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 extends v1's YTSeg-only coverage to AMI multi-party meeting segmentation, including training and evaluation in this distinct domain. It also tests explicit timestamp prediction with and without transcription. Title generation itself was already present in v1.

E2.justification: Table A11 adds BART as a title-quality comparison reference, with results attributed to Retkowski and Waibel (2024). Its oracle segmentation and reference-transcript setting are explicitly identified. The original segmentation comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds AMI-only versus YTSeg-to-AMI training comparisons, short-meeting and all-meeting evaluations, T1 evaluation at 8/10/12 seconds, and T2 scoring at ±3/±6 seconds. It also introduces temporal-matching and global-concatenation title evaluation using BERTScore and ROUGE-L. Original six-second evaluations and documented training settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test pretraining transfer to AMI, sensitivity to evaluation granularity, and timestamp-localization errors using predicted versus forced-alignment timestamps. Duration analysis gains segment-density and speaker-composition statistics. Existing acoustic-feature, DeepFilterNet and MLLM failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Existing plot bands and dataset summary reporting are retained. Neither new run counts or seeds nor new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are documented. Added performance tables report point scores.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial AMI, timestamp, title-quality, granularity and continuous-time results. For example, Table 7 reports 12.52 F1 using Qwen3-Omni's predicted timestamps versus 43.84 using forced alignment of the same outputs. Table A8 reveals AudioSeg/MiniSeg-with-features ranking reversals at 8/10 seconds. Original table scores are retained; Section 5.1 corrects 37.74 to 37.76, matching the unchanged Table 4.

T1.justification: New Appendix B formally defines temporal title matching through endpoint tolerances and global title comparison through chronological concatenation, including unequal chapter counts. Existing segmentation definitions and alignment mathematics remain unchanged; no proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, three stated contributions and conclusion retain their scientific claims about AudioSeg, acoustic cues, ASR robustness and transcript-invariant evaluation. The added experiments support and investigate these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 identifies temporal localization as an MLLM bottleneck, interprets transfer to meetings, explains re-discretization artifacts, and connects duration with speaker complexity. It also adds an explanation for adapted encoders' weaker standalone performance. Limitations now acknowledge small-scale AMI validation while retaining generalization concerns.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future AudioSeg release; v2 reports its release and supplies a model-access link in the first-page footnote. Existing hyperparameters, hardware information, prompts and feature-extraction details are retained across appendix renumbering. Availability is reported by the PDF, not externally verified.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds positioning against VAD and ASR chunking, while Appendix B discusses prior segmentation and title-evaluation approaches. Additional citations cover AMI, downstream chapter applications and encoder adaptation. The central novelty framing remains stable.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language and cross-reference corrections, adds a temporal-grounding research question and subsection, and inserts a title-quality appendix. Subsequent sections and appendices are renumbered, while most existing prose and the overall organization are retained.

P2.justification: The results presentation expands substantially: Table 7 gains a timestamp-variant block and explanatory notes, and new appendix tables display AMI comparisons, granularity sensitivity, continuous-time scores, title metrics and duration statistics. Existing figures and tables are retained, with several relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's single-dataset evidence and six-second main evaluation through AMI transfer tests and granularity/continuous-time checks (Tables A5–A9). Its same-output timestamp analysis also identifies a concrete MLLM failure mechanism. These additions address important validation gaps. Small AMI samples, ranking exceptions under re-discretization and an unspecified title-matching tolerance limit the conclusions, but the overall gain in empirical support and diagnosis is substantial.
